title: Booting: From Power Button to Desktop
summary: When the power comes on, the CPU starts running firmware from a chip on the motherboard (UEFI, once BIOS), which checks the hardware and loads a boot loader from the disk. The boot loader loads the kernel, the kernel starts its drivers and the first process, and that process starts everything else, ending with the login screen.
markdown:
## The chicken-and-egg problem The operating system lives on the disk. Reading the disk needs a program. But when the power comes on, RAM is empty: there is no program yet. How does a computer start? The answer is a chain of small programs, each loading a bigger one. This is called **booting**, from "pulling yourself up by your bootstraps". ```mermaid flowchart TB P["Power on"] --> F["1. Firmware (UEFI)
from a chip on the motherboard"] F --> B["2. Boot loader
from the disk"] B --> K["3. Kernel
loaded into RAM"] K --> I["4. First process
(init / systemd, or Windows' session manager)"] I --> S["5. Services, login screen, desktop"] ``` ## 1. Firmware The CPU is built to start fetching instructions from one fixed address when it powers on. That address is wired to a small **flash memory chip** on the motherboard that holds the **firmware**: on PCs since about 2010, **UEFI**; before that, the **BIOS** (from the original IBM PC). The firmware: - tests the hardware (the **POST**, power-on self test: is there RAM? a keyboard?); - sets up the essentials: memory, the clock, the CPU's settings; - finds a disk to boot from, in the order set in its settings; - loads the **boot loader** from that disk into RAM and jumps to it. With **Secure Boot**, UEFI checks that the boot loader is digitally signed by a trusted maker before running it, so malware cannot slip in before the operating system starts. ## 2. The boot loader The boot loader is a small program whose job is to find the kernel and load it. Examples: **Windows Boot Manager**, **GRUB** (Linux), and Apple's **iBoot**. It may show a menu to choose between operating systems. It reads the kernel file from the file system into RAM, along with a small starter set of drivers, and jumps to the kernel's first instruction. ## 3. The kernel starts The kernel now takes over the machine: - switches the CPU into its full 64-bit mode and sets up virtual memory (6.03); - starts its drivers and detects devices; - mounts the main file system (makes the disk's files reachable); - starts the scheduler (6.02); - starts the **first user-mode process**. ## 4. The first process On Linux the first process has PID **1**: usually **systemd** (or the older **init**). Every other process on the system descends from it, through `fork` and `execve` (6.04). It starts the background **services** - networking, sound, printing, logging - and finally the login screen. Windows does the same with its Session Manager and Winlogon. ## 5. Login and desktop You log in; the system starts your desktop (Explorer on Windows, Finder and the Dock on macOS, GNOME or KDE on Linux) and your startup apps. From power button to desktop, on a modern computer with an SSD, takes about 10 to 20 seconds. ## Sleep, hibernate, shut down | | What happens | Starting again | |---|---|---| | **Sleep** | RAM stays powered and keeps everything; the rest switches off | Instant: everything is still in RAM | | **Hibernate** | RAM's contents are written to the disk, then the power goes off | Slower: RAM is reloaded from the disk | | **Shut down** | Programs are closed, files saved, power off | A full boot | > [!info] Phones boot the same way > A phone has its own firmware and boot loader (with signature checks at every step, so only the maker's software can run), then a Linux kernel (Android) or Apple's XNU kernel (iOS), then the first process and the home screen. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Where does the very first code run after power-on come from? - The hard drive + Firmware in a chip on the motherboard - RAM > RAM is empty at power-on; the CPU starts at an address wired to the firmware chip (UEFI or BIOS). ? What is the boot loader's job? - To test the hardware - To show the desktop + To load the kernel and start it > It finds the kernel on the disk, loads it into RAM and jumps to it. Examples: GRUB, Windows Boot Manager, iBoot. ? On Linux, what is process number 1? - The kernel itself + The first user-mode process - The desktop > Usually systemd, which starts everything else; every other process descends from it. ? What is the difference between sleep and hibernate? - There is no difference + Sleep keeps RAM powered; hibernate does not - Hibernate is faster to wake from > Hibernate saves RAM to disk and powers off completely. Sleep wakes instantly but uses a little power. ```

cards.q: Where does the very first code run after power-on come from?
cards.a:
Firmware in a chip on the motherboard

RAM is empty at power-on; the CPU starts at an address wired to the firmware chip (UEFI or BIOS).

cards.q: What is the boot loader's job?
cards.a:
To load the kernel and start it

It finds the kernel on the disk, loads it into RAM and jumps to it. Examples: GRUB, Windows Boot Manager, iBoot.

cards.q: On Linux, what is process number 1?
cards.a:
The first user-mode process

Usually systemd, which starts everything else; every other process descends from it.

cards.q: What is the difference between sleep and hibernate?
cards.a:
Sleep keeps RAM powered; hibernate does not

Hibernate saves RAM to disk and powers off completely. Sleep wakes instantly but uses a little power.
